newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU parliament to vote on fuel/car emissions rules.
newsitem.headline: EU parliament to vote on fuel/car emissions rules.

text.p: Draft EU rules on fuel quality and engine emission standards are likely to come under fire for being too weak on Wednesday, when the European Parliament debates its response to European Commission proposals.

Discussions will centre on two reports, adopted last month by the parliament's environment committee, which urged the beefing up of two proposals to improve fuel quality and cut various vehicle pollutants by two thirds by 2010.

French Green Noel Mamere and German Socialist Bernd Lange, who wrote the reports on proposals on fuels and for emission norms for petrol and diesel-engined vehicles respectively, criticised the use of flawed cost estimates and poor data on localised urban peaks in air pollution.

Among the changes they advocated are stricter fuel quality norms, particularly lower sulphur content in diesel, and compulsory 2005 standards in place of the Commission's proposal for non-binding targets.
Other changes would include engine emissions testing from start-up and at sub-zero temperatures and doubling the required durability of new vehicles' anti-pollution equipment.

The oil industry has attacked the proposed amendments on fuel as likely to cost billions of dollars in extra refinery costs, while European carmakers opposed any tightening of proposed standards for 2000 and 2005, which they said are already enough to meet international health norms.

Wednesday's debate, to be followed by a vote the same day or on Thursday, will complete parliament's first reading of the texts and leave the way open for EU environment ministers to reach a provisional agreement on the texts at a meeting in June.

National positions vary from those of Greece, Spain, Italy and Portugal, who think the original Commission proposals are too tough, to those of Sweden, Finland, Austria and Denmark, who want various bits strengthened.

Whatever their divisions, national positions are far removed from proposals under scrutiny in parliament, a gulf which industry lobbyists, EU officials and various Euro-MPs see as pointing inevitably to a final deal emerging from "conciliation procedure" negotiations early next year.
They say positions adopted this week in Strasbourg and in June should therefore be seen as opening shots in that debate.
